planting.note: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch below soil level in fertile, well-drained soil in full sun; this late-season rebloomer rewards consistent moisture through summer with a strong extended bloom.

directions: Registered by hybridizer Margo Reed in 1997 from a cross of So Lovely and Olallie Lois, After Awhile Crocodile bears light rose self flowers with a clean lemon throat, each bloom about five and a half inches across on scapes roughly 28 inches tall. It is a semi-evergreen extended bloomer and an early-morning opener, flowering especially late in the season and extending color after most earlier cultivars have finished, which earned it the American Hemerocallis Society's Eugene S. Foster Award for outstanding late bloomer in 2005 along with an Honorable Mention the same year. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.

planting.note: Plant divisions with the crown about an inch below soil level in average, well-drained soil in full sun; established clumps need little beyond routine division to keep flowering heavily.

directions: Hybridized by Geraldine L. Couturier and registered in 1992, Loch Ness Monster bears large lavender flowers about seven and a half inches across with a dark mauve halo fading into a yellow-green throat, each petal marked with a pale pin-stripe down the midrib, carried on scapes around 25 inches tall. This dormant diploid blooms in midseason and was later used as a cross parent behind the Oz-themed cultivar Ocean Spirit, and it went on to earn an American Hemerocallis Society Honorable Mention in 2008. Divide congested clumps every three to four years in spring to sustain vigorous flowering.
